en: Tattvasamāsasūtravṛttiḥ:
Homage to that great seer Kapila, who, at the time of the primordial creation, attained knowledge through birth regarding the twenty-five principles. (1)
Now, therefore, we shall explain the Sāṅkhya aphorisms known as the *Tattvasamāsa*.

Here, a certain Brāhmaṇa, overcome by the three kinds of suffering, sought refuge with the great seer Kapila, the teacher of Sāṅkhya. Having announced his lineage, name, gotra, and sacred study, he spoke:
“Bhagavān, what is the supreme here? What is reality as it truly is? By doing what would one have accomplished all that is to be done? Kapila said: “I shall explain.
There are eight primordial natures (prakṛtis). [Tattvasamāsasūtra 1]
The sixteen transformations. (Tats_2)
The person. (Tats_3)
The state of being composed of the three qualities (traiguṇya). // TS 4 //
Wandering. // Tats_5 //
The process of reabsorption. // 6 //
The internal, the elemental, and the divine. // Tats_7 //
The five higher knowledges. // Tats_8 //
The five sources of action. (Tats_9)
The five winds. //Tats_10//
The five [elements] have action as their essence. //Tats_11//
Ignorance has five joints. (Tattvasaṃgraha 12)
Incapacity is of twenty-eight kinds. (Tattvasaṃgraha 13)
Contentment is ninefold. (Tattvasaṃgraha 14)
Accomplishment is eightfold. // 15 //
The fundamental meanings are tenfold. (Tats_16)
The creation of favor. //Tattvasaṃgraha 17//
The creation of beings is of fourteen kinds. (Tattvasaṃgraha 18)
The creation of the realms is threefold. (Tats_19)
Bondage is threefold. (Tattvasaṃgraha 20)
Liberation is threefold. (Tattvasaṃgraha 21)
The means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) is threefold. // 22 //
Suffering is threefold. (Tattvasaṃgraha 23)
Having correctly understood this reality through this lineage, one becomes one who has accomplished all that was to be done and is no longer overcome by the threefold suffering.
Thus ends the Sāṅkhya-sūtras known as the Tattvasamāsa.
[The eight primal natures.
Now, as to what the eight primal natures (prakṛti) are, it is said here:
the unmanifest (avyakta), intellect (buddhi), ego-consciousness (ahaṅkāra), and the five subtle elements (tanmātra)—these are the eight primal natures.

In this regard, the unmanifest (avyakta) is first explained: just as in the world jars, cloths, walls, beds, and so forth are manifested, that which is not manifested in such a way is called "unmanifest.
The meaning is that it is not perceived by the sense organs, such as the ear and the rest.
Why? Because it is without beginning, middle, or end, and because it is partless.
Soundless, touchless, formless, imperishable, and likewise eternal; devoid of taste and smell;
without beginning or middle; beyond the Great (mahat); fixed—this is what the wise proclaim as Pradhāna.
Subtle, without marks, insentient, without beginning or end, likewise characterized by productivity, partless, one, and indeed common to all—this is the Unmanifest (avyakta).
These are the synonymous terms for the Unmanifest:
the Unmanifest, Pradhāna, Brahman, the Supreme, the Fixed, the Multiplier, the Imperishable, the Field, and that which is produced from darkness (tamas).
What is said here to be intellect? Intellect is determination; this determination is that from which there arises the cognition of substances such as cows and so forth.
It is thus and not otherwise: this is indeed a cow, not a horse;
this is indeed a post, not a person.
Such is this intellect (*buddhi*).
This intellect, moreover, has eight forms: virtue (*dharma*), knowledge (*jñāna*), dispassion (*vairāgya*), and sovereignty (*aiśvarya*).

Among these, that which is called virtue is the opposite of non-virtue; it is prescribed by the *Śruti* and *Smṛti*, not contradicted by the conduct of the learned (*śiṣṭa*), and characterized by auspiciousness.

Knowledge is the opposite of ignorance; it is the thorough awakening to the true nature of existing things. Dispassion is the opposite of non-dispassion; it is the lack of attachment toward objects such as sound and the rest.
Sovereignty is the opposite of lack of sovereignty; it consists of the eight qualities beginning with atomization (*aṇimā*).

These four are the *sāttvika* [qualities]. Adharma, ignorance (*ajñāna*), non-detachment (*avairāgya*), and lack of mastery (*anaiśvarya*). Adharma is the opposite of dharma; it is contrary to the *Śruti* and *Smṛti*, opposed to the conduct of the virtuous, and characterized by inauspiciousness.
Ignorance is the opposite of knowledge; it is the lack of comprehension regarding the true nature of reality and of beings.
Lack of dispassion (*avairāgya*) is the opposite of dispassion; it is attachment to objects such as sound and the rest.
Lack of sovereignty (*anaiśvarya*) is the opposite of sovereignty; it is the state of being devoid of the powers such as *aṇimā* (minuteness) and so forth.
These are the four *tāmasa* [forms of error].
In that regard, upward movement occurs through the sign of dharma;
liberation through the sign of knowledge;
and dissolution into primordial nature through the sign of dispassion.
By means of sovereignty as its cause, one's movement becomes unimpeded.
Thus, this intellect (buddhi) has been explained as having eight forms.
These are the synonymous terms for intellect.
Mind, intellect, the Great One (Mahat), Brahmā, renown, wisdom, sacred learning, fortitude, discernment,
continuity, memory, thought, and intelligence are all declared to be synonyms for the intellect (buddhi).
Here it is asked: what is called "I-making" (ahaṅkāra)? It is answered: conceit is ahaṅkāra;
[it is the thought] "I am in sound," "I am in touch," "I am in form," "I am in taste."
"I am the fragrance; I am the master; I am the wealthy one; I am the lord. // 1 //
"I am an enjoyer; I am consecrated in the Dharma; he has been slain by me;
I shall slay [others] with superior forces"—such are the thoughts that arise. (2)
That which is this cognition of self-conceit (abhimāna) is the ego-sense (ahaṅkāra).
These are the synonymous terms for the ego-sense:
the ego-sense as the "transformative" (vaikārika), the "fiery" (taijasa), the "source of elements" (bhūtādi), the "with inference" (sānumāna), and the "without inference" (niranumāna).

Here it is asked: what are the five subtle elements (*tanmātras*)? It is said: the five subtle elements associated with the ego (*ahaṅkāra*) are the subtle element of sound (*śabda-tanmātra*), the subtle element of touch (*sparśa-tanmātra*), the subtle element of form (*rūpa-tanmātra*), the subtle element of taste (*rasa-tanmātra*), and the subtle element of smell (*gandha-tanmātra*). Among these, first, the subtle elements of sound are perceived only within sounds; they are perceived as specific qualities of sound, such as acute (*udātta*), grave (*anudātta*), circumflex (*svarita*), tremulous (*kampita*), and the musical notes (*svara*)—ṣaḍja, ṛṣabha, gāndhāra, madhyama, pañcama, dhaivata, niṣāda, and so forth.
Therefore, there is no specific distinction within the sound-tanmātra.
Now, the touch-tanmātras are perceived only among tactile objects; therein, specific distinctions of touch such as soft, hard, rough, slippery, cold, hot, and so forth, are perceived.
Therefore, there is no specific distinction within the touch-tanmātra.
The subtle elements of form (rūpa-tanmātra) are perceived only within forms.
Therein, specific varieties of form—such as white, red, black, green, yellow, turmeric-yellow, and madder-red—are perceived.
Therefore, there is no distinction within the subtle element of form itself.
Likewise, the subtle elements of taste (rasatanmātra) are perceived only within tastes.
Therein, specific varieties of taste such as pungent, bitter, astringent, alkaline, sweet, sour, and salty are perceived.
Therefore, there is no distinction [of these qualities] within the subtle element of taste.
Now, in the subtle elements of smell, only smell is perceived;
therein, specific smells—both fragrant and foul—are perceived.
Therefore, there is no distinction within the subtle element of smell itself.
Thus, these five subtle elements (tanmātras) have been indicated.
Now, their synonymous terms are as follows:

they are called *tanmātras*, *aviśeṣas*, the primal natures (*prakṛtis*) of the gross elements (*mahābhūtas*), objects of experience (*bhogyas*), atoms (*aṇavas*), and those that are calm (*śānta*), terrible (*ghora*), or delusive (*mūḍha*).
Thus, these eight primary natures (prakṛtis)—designated as the unmanifest (avyakta), intellect (buddhi), ego (ahaṃkāra), and the subtle elements (tanmātra)—have been explained.
Now, why are they called "primary natures"? They are called primary natures because they produce (prakurvanti).
[The sixteen transformations // Tats_2 //] Now, as to what those sixteen transformations are, it is said here:
the eleven faculties and the five great elements— these are the sixteen transformations.
In this context, the sense faculties (indriya) are first described.
The ear, the skin, the two eyes, the tongue, and the nose constitute the five sense faculties of cognition (buddhīndriya).
The ear grasps its own object, sound; the skin [grasps] the object of touch; the eye [grasps] the object of form; the tongue [grasps] the object of taste; and the nose [grasps] the object of smell.
The five organs of action, known as speech, hands, feet, anus, and genitals, each perform their respective functions.
Among them, speech utters words;
the two hands perform actions.
The feet are movement; the anus is excretion;
the genitals are pleasure.
The mind is of a dual nature;
it performs the functions of its own volition and conceptualization.
Thus, the eleven sense organs have been explained.
Now, their synonyms are:

*indriyāṇi* (senses), *karaṇāni* (instruments), *vaikārikāṇi* (evolutes), *khāni* (cavities), *niyatāni* (fixed), *padāni* (stations), *avadhṛtāni* (determined), *aṇūni* (subtle), and *akṣāṇi* (organs).
Now, as to what the five great elements (*pañcamahābhūtāni*) are, it is said here:
Earth, water, fire, air, and space are the great elements (*mahābhūta*).
Among them, earth functions by way of supporting and provides assistance to the other four. Water, functioning by way of cohesion, provides assistance to the other four.
Fire, functioning through its nature as a cooker, provides assistance to the four [great elements].
Wind, functioning through its nature as a mover, provides assistance to the four.
Space, functioning by providing room, provides assistance to the four.
Earth possesses five qualities: sound, touch, form, taste, and smell.
Water possesses four qualities: sound, touch, form, and taste.
Fire possesses three qualities: sound, touch, and form.
Wind possesses sound and touch and has two qualities; space possesses sound and has one quality. Thus have the five great elements been described.
Now, their synonyms are as follows:

the elements (bhūtāni), the specific forms of the elements (bhūtaviśeṣāḥ), modifications (vikārāḥ), configurations (ākṛtayaḥ), bodies (tanavaḥ), physical forms (vigrahāḥ), the tranquil (śāntāḥ), the terrible (ghorāḥ), and the deluded (mūḍhāḥ). These sixteen modifications have been explained. [The Puruṣa. (Tattvasaṃgraha 3)
Then he asks: "What is called the Puruṣa? It is said:

The Puruṣa is beginningless, subtle, all-pervading, conscious, devoid of qualities (aguṇa), eternal, the seer, the enjoyer, the non-doer, the knower of the field (kṣetravit), stainless, and characterized by the absence of procreation.

Then he asks: "Why is he called Puruṣa? Because he is ancient (purāṇāt), because he dwells in the city (puri-śayanāt), and because he functions as the domestic priest (purohita-vṛttitvāt), he is called Puruṣa.
Now, why is it beginningless?
It is called "beginningless" because its beginning, end, or middle is not found.
Why is it subtle?
It is subtle because it is partless and beyond the reach of the senses.
Why is it all-pervading? It is called all-pervading because it has reached everything; there is no space that is not occupied by it.
Why is it conscious?
Because it possesses the perception of pleasure, pain, and delusion.
Why is it devoid of qualities (guṇa)?
Because the qualities of sattva, rajas, and tamas do not exist in it, it is "without qualities" (aguṇa).
Why is it eternal? Because it is uncreated and because it is non-productive.
Why is it the seer?
"Because of the non-perception of nature and its transformations.
Why is it the enjoyer?
Because of its conscious nature and because of its thorough knowledge of pleasure and pain.
Why is he a non-doer?
Because of his indifference and because he is devoid of the qualities (guṇas).
Why is he the knower of the field?
One who knows the qualities of the fields is called the "knower of the fields" (*kṣetravit*).
Now, why is he stainless?
He is stainless because auspicious and inauspicious karmas do not exist within this person.
Why is it of a nature not to produce?
Because it is seedless;
the meaning is that it does not produce anything at all.
Thus has this *sāṃkhya-puruṣa* been explained. Now, the synonyms for this *puruṣa* are:
*puruṣa*, *ātman*, *pumān*, *puṃguṇa*, *bahula*, *jantu*, *jīva*, *kṣetrajña*, *nara*, *kavi*, *brahman*, *akṣara*, *prāṇa*, *aja*, *yaḥ*, *kaḥ*, *saḥ*, and *eṣaḥ*.
Thus these twenty-five principles have been explained:
the eight primal natures, the sixteen transformations, and the person (puruṣa).
One who knows the twenty-five principles is liberated, regardless of which stage of life he follows—whether he has matted hair, a shaven head, or a topknot; of this there is no doubt.
Here it is asked: Is the Puruṣa the agent or the non-agent?
If the Puruṣa were the agent, then he would perform auspicious deeds.
But surely, three types of activity are observed in the world belonging to the Puruṣa; therefore, is it not established that the agency belongs to the Guṇas?
The sattvic modification consists of contentment known as dharma, the practice of restraints and observances, renown, knowledge, sovereignty, dispassion, and illumination.
Passion, anger, greed, disparaging others, extreme ferocity, discontent, distorted appearance, and harshness— this is known as the passionate (rājasa) temperament.
Negligence, intoxication, despondency, atheism, addiction to women, sleep, laziness,
cruelty, and impurity— this is the tamasic mode of conduct.
Having observed these three functions in the world, it is established that the qualities (guṇas) possess agency; thus, the person (puruṣa) is established as being non-agent.

Due to a perverted vision caused by rajas and tamas, the ignorant person, lacking mastery even over the bending of a blade of grass, falsely imagines, "I am the doer," regarding these qualities of nature as they proceed.

Saying "all this was done by me" and "this is mine," the ignorant person, out of conceit, becomes like a madman acting as an agent; regarding this, it is said: "All actions performed in every way by the qualities of nature, the self whose mind is deluded by egoism thinks, 'I am the doer.'"
Because it is beginningless and devoid of qualities, O Kaunteya, this immutable Supreme Self, even while dwelling in the body, neither acts nor is tainted.
Thus,
he who sees that actions are being performed in every way by nature alone,
and likewise sees the self as the non-doer, he truly sees.

Regarding this, it is asked: "Is this Puruṣa one, or are there many? It is stated that the plurality of Puruṣas is established because of the diversity of pleasure, pain, and delusion; because of the mixture and purification [of qualities]; because of the proficiency of the instruments [of perception]; and because of birth, death, and the various instruments [of action]. Furthermore, it is established by the distinctions of the world, stages of life (āśrama), and social classes (varṇa). If there were only one Puruṣa, then when one person is happy, everyone would be happy.
If one were suffering, all would suffer;
if one possessed proficiency in action, all would possess proficiency in action;
and if one were born, all would be born.
If one were dead, all would die;
yet this is not so, for many persons are established from this [evidence]:

because there is a plurality of *liṅgas* (subtle bodies) in the division of the body, which involves the conjunction of the generic form (*ākṛti*), the womb, the state of being, and the physical frame.
Thus, first of all, the Sāṃkhya teachers—Kapila, Āsuri, Pañcaśikha, Patañjali, and others—describe many puruṣas;
whereas the Vedānta teachers—Hari, Hara, Hiraṇyagarbha, Vyāsa, and others—describe the self as being only one.
Why is it so? To this he says:
The Person alone is all this—whatever has been and whatever is to be;
he is also the lord of immortality, which surpasses everything else.
That indeed is fire, that is the sun, that is the wind, and that is the moon;
that is the pure, that is Brahman, that is the waters, and he is Prajāpati.
That alone is truth, that is the immortal, that is liberation, and that is the supreme goal.
That is the Imperishable, that is the most excellent boon of Savitṛ,
than which there is nothing higher or further beyond.
Because there is nothing smaller or greater than He, standing alone like a tree, fixed in heaven— by that Puruṣa all this is pervaded.
With hands and feet everywhere, with eyes, heads, and faces everywhere,
and with ears everywhere in the world, He stands encompassing all.
Manifesting the qualities of all the senses, yet devoid of all senses;
the Lord and Sovereign of all, the great refuge of everything.
The sages know that Brahman to be that in which all principles, the self of all, the source of all, and everything itself dissolve from every side.
For the self of all beings is indeed one alone, residing in body after body;
it is seen as both one and many, like the moon reflected in water.
For that one Great Self dwells within all beings, both stationary and moving, by whom all this is pervaded.
This Self is one for all the worlds, yet it has been made manifold by one;
they speak of the Self as distinct only in the context of the engagement with knowledge and other faculties.
The wise look with equanimity upon a Brahmin, a worm, an insect, an outcaste, a dog, an elephant, a beast, a gadfly, and a mosquito.
Just as a single thread passes through gold,
and likewise through pearls, gems, coral, clay, and silver;
In the same way among cows, among humans, and likewise among elephants, deer, and so forth,
this one Self alone is to be known as established everywhere.
[The three qualities (traiguṇya).
Here it is asked: what is meant by the term "the three qualities"? It is the three qualities—sattva, rajas, and tamas—themselves that constitute "the three qualities."

That which is called *sattva* is characterized by clarity, lightness, serenity, attachment, joy, contentment, endurance, satisfaction, and so forth; it has infinite subdivisions, but in brief, its nature is happiness.
That which is called *rajas* is characterized by grief, distress, perspiration, paralysis, agitation, anger, pride, and so forth; it has infinite subdivisions, but in brief, its nature is suffering.

That which is called *tamas* is characterized by concealment, obstruction, loathsomeness, dejection, heaviness, laziness, sleep, negligence, and so forth; it has infinite subdivisions, but in brief, its nature is delusion.

This triad of qualities has been explained. One should know that *sattva* is illuminating, one should know that *rajas* is impelling, and one should know that *tamas* is non-illuminating; this is what is designated as the "triad of qualities."
[The evolution (sañcara). // Tattvasaṃgraha 5 //] [The dissolution (pratisañcara). // Tattvasaṃgraha 6 //] Here it is asked: what is evolution and what is dissolution?
To this it is replied:
there is origination, evolution, dissolution, and re-evolution.

Among these, "origination" refers to the arising of the intellect (*buddhi*), which—presided over by the Supreme Puruṣa—is produced from the Unmanifest (*avyakta*) previously described as the source of all.
The intellect possesses eight qualities.
From the principle of intellect (buddhitattva), the ego-sense (ahaṅkāra) arises;
and that ego-sense is threefold: the sattvic (vaikārika), the rājasic (taijasa), and the tāmasic (bhūtādi).
In that regard, the sense organs arise from the *vaikārika* ego alone; the subtle elements arise from the *bhūtādi*;
and both arise from the *taijasa*.
From the subtle elements (tanmātras) arise the gross elements; this is the process of evolution (sañcara).
The process of dissolution (pratisañcara) is as follows: the gross elements dissolve into the subtle elements, and the subtle elements and the sense organs dissolve into the ego-sense (ahaṃkāra).
Egoity dissolves into the intellect;
the intellect dissolves into the unmanifest; that unmanifest does not dissolve into anything whatsoever.

Why? Because they are unproduced; know that both *prakṛti* and *puru�șa* are indeed beginningless. Thus has the process of dissolution (*pratisañcara*) been explained—both with respect to the internal (*adhyātma*), the elemental (*adhibhūta*), and the divine (*adhidaivata*).
Regarding this, he asks: "What is that which is internal, elemental, and divine?"
Regarding this, it is said: Intellect is the internal self (adhyātma); that which is to be known is the elemental principle (adhibhūta); and Brahmā is the presiding deity therein (adhidaivata).
The ego (ahaṃkāra) is the internal self; that which is to be thought about is the elemental principle; and Rudra is the presiding deity therein.

The mind is the internal; that which is to be conceptualized is the elemental; the moon is the presiding deity therein. The ear is the internal; that which is to be heard is the elemental; space is the presiding deity therein. The skin is the internal; that which is to be touched is the elemental; wind is the presiding deity therein.

The eye is the internal; that which is to be seen is the elemental; the sun is the presiding deity therein. The tongue is the internal; that which is to be tasted is the elemental; Varuṇa is the presiding deity therein. The nose is the internal; that which is to be smelled is the elemental; the earth is the presiding deity therein.

Speech is the internal self (adhyātma); that which is to be spoken is the external element (adhibhūta); and Agni is the presiding deity there (adhidaivata). The hands are the internal self; that which is to be grasped is the external element; and Indra is the presiding deity there. The feet are the internal self; that which is to be traversed is the external element; and Viṣṇu is the presiding deity there.

The anus is the internal self; that which is to be evacuated is the elemental sphere; Mitra is the presiding deity therein. The organ of generation is the internal self; that which is to be enjoyed for pleasure is the elemental sphere; Prajāpati is the presiding deity therein.
Thus, the internal self, the elemental sphere, and the presiding deity of this thirteenfold instrument have been explained.

He who knows the principles as they truly are—their nature as the qualities (guṇas) and their presiding deities—is freed from evil and the multitude of defects; he experiences the qualities but is not attached to them by the qualities.
[The five masteries (pañcābhibuddhayaḥ). Now, what are those five masteries? They are said to be: resolve, conceit, desire, the sense of duty, and action.

The activity of the intellect (*buddhi*) is the resolve that "this is to be done by me," directed toward the object of cognition. Egoism (*ahaṃkāra*), which is the conceit directed toward the notions of one's own self and the nature of others, is the activity of the intellect. Desire, longing, and volition are the activities of the mind (*manas*).
The function of the sense organs (*buddhīndriya*) consists of the cognitive activity characterized by the perception of objects such as sound and the acts of hearing and so forth;
the function of the organs of action (*karmendriya*) consists of the cognitive activity characterized by speaking and so forth.
Thus, these five forms of apprehension (*abhibuddhi*) have been explained.
[The five sources of action // Tats_9 //] Now, what are these five sources of action? They are said to be:
steadfastness (*dhṛti*), faith (*śraddhā*), happiness (*sukha*), the desire to know (*avividiṣā*), and the desire to know (*vividiṣā*); these are the five sources of action.
Having resolved upon external duties, he who protects what has been acquired,
being intent on that and established in that— this indeed is the characteristic of fortitude (dhṛti).
Vedic study, celibacy, performing sacrifices, officiating at sacrifices,
austerity, giving gifts, receiving gifts, and burnt offerings are recorded as the characteristics of faith.
But she who practices the duties and austerities of a Brahmin for the sake of happiness,
and is constantly devoted to expiatory rites— she is proclaimed to be Sukhā.
The internal organ being mixed with the honey of sense-objects is the state of non-desire for knowledge (*avividiṣā*);
and for meditators, desire for knowledge (*vividiṣā*) is the source of wisdom. Unity and diversity, as well as permanence and insentience, are likewise [to be understood].
The effect exists in a subtle state and is unshakeable; that is to be known as the desire for knowledge.
The desire to know [the world] (*vividiṣā*), which brings about the exhaustion of cause and effect, is the natural disposition (*prākṛtikī vṛttiḥ*).
Fortitude, faith, and happiness constitute the "desire not to know" (*avividiṣā*); these four lead to bondage, while the single desire to know leads to liberation.
Thus, these five sources of action (*karmayoni*) have been explained.
[The five winds // Tats_10 //] Here it is asked: what are the five winds said to be? They are prāṇa, apāna, samāna, udāna, and vyāna.

Thus, these are the five vital airs (vāyu) within the bodies of embodied beings. Among them, the air called *prāṇa* presides over the mouth and nose; it is designated as *prāṇa* because of its leading forward (*praṇayana*) and its departing (*prakramaṇa*). The air called *apāna* is situated at the navel; it is designated as *apāna* because of its carrying away (*apanayana*) and its downward movement (*adhogamana*).
The wind called *samāna* has its seat in the heart; it is designated as *samāna* because it brings things together and causes them to meet.
The wind called *udāna* has its seat in the throat; it is designated as *udāna* because of its upward movement and its departure from the body.
The wind called *vyāna* has its seat in the joints; it is designated as *vyāna* because of its pervasive distribution and its expansion.
Thus the five winds have been explained. [They are the nature of the five functions.
Here it is asked: what are those five that constitute the nature of the functions? It is said in response:
The *vaikārika*, the *taijasa*, and the *bhūtādi* are both with inference (*sānumāna*) and without inference (*niranumāna*).
Among them, the *vaikārika* is the performer of auspicious actions;
the *taijasa* is the performer of inauspicious actions.
The originator of the elements is the performer of deluded action;

the one accompanied by inference is the performer of auspiciously deluded action; and the one devoid of inference is the performer of inauspiciously deluded action. Thus, the five types of selves characterized by their actions have been explained.

[Ignorance with five sections // TS 12 //] Here it is asked: what is this ignorance with five sections? It is said: darkness (*tamas*), delusion (*moha*), great delusion (*mahāmoha*), gloom (*tāmisra*), and blinding darkness (*andhatāmisra*).
Among those, both *tamas* and *moha* consist of eight forms each;
*mahāmoha* consists of ten forms;
and *tāmisra* and *andhatāmisra* consist of eighteen forms each.

*Tamas* is defined as the conceit of self (*ātma-abhimāna*) with respect to that which is not the self—namely, the eight *prakṛtis* designated as the unmanifest (*avyakta*), intellect (*buddhi*), ego (*ahaṃkāra*), and the five subtle elements (*tanmātra*).
*Moha* is defined as the conceit that arises for the sake of attaining the eightfold sovereignty beginning with *aṇimā*.

*Mahāmoha* is defined as when one thinks "I am liberated" regarding the ten functions consisting of the objects of sense, such as sound and so forth, both those perceived and those heard from tradition.

*Tāmisra* is the name for the unhindered hatred toward the eightfold sovereignty beginning with *aṇimā* and toward the tenfold objects of experience; the suffering that arises therein is designated as *tāmisra*.

*Andhatāmisra* is the name for the despondency that arises at the time of death when the eightfold sovereignty beginning with *aṇimā* and the tenfold objects have been accomplished; that is designated as *andhatāmisra*.
Thus, this ignorance (*avidyā*) with its five sections has been explained in its sixty-two divisions.
[The powerlessness is of twenty-eight kinds // Tattvasaṃgraha 13 //] Here it is asked: what is this twenty-eightfold powerlessness? It is said here:
the eleven impairments of the sense organs, and the seventeen impairments of contentment and accomplishment (buddhi).
This is the twenty-eightfold incapacity (*aśakti*).
Among these, the impairments of the sense faculties (*indriyavadha*) are first described:
deafness in the ear, insensibility in the tongue, leprosy in the skin, blindness in the eye, and loss of smell in the nose.

Muteness in speech, deformity of the hands, lameness of the feet, paralysis of the organ of speech, impotence of the organ of generation, and insanity of the mind—these are the eleven impairments of the faculties.
(There are nine kinds of contentment. [Tattvasaṃgraha 14]
[The eightfold accomplishment.
(Tats_15) The seventeen forms of the destruction of contentment and accomplishment are the opposites of contentment and accomplishment.
First, the opposites of contentment are stated:
In that regard, the infinite conviction that "Pradhāna does not exist" is ignorance;
likewise, the state of being dissolved in the darkness of self-knowledge as "I am," and the non-perception of the ego-sense (ahaṅkāra), are ignorance;
and the failure to perceive that the subtle elements (tanmātras) truly exist as the causes of the gross elements is ignorance.
Engagement in the acquisition of sense objects is difficult to cross;
engagement in their preservation is impossible to cross;
and engagement with wealth while failing to see the fault of its depletion is difficult to lead across.
"Enjoyments are like a mirage for one lacking power;
for one who does not perceive the fault of violence, the undertaking of enjoyments is like a mirage in water.
Thus, the nine types of discontent, which are the opposites of contentment, have been explained.

Now, the eight non-attainments (*asiddhi*), which are the opposites of attainment (*siddhi*), are described. "Atāra" refers to the manifestation of unity within the diversity of the elements (*bhūta*). "Āsutāra" is the grasping of a meaning contrary to what was heard from the mere sound [of the words]; for example, having heard that "one who knows diversity is liberated," one understands it perversely as "one who knows diversity is indeed not liberated."

Even for one intent upon study and listening, if the realization of the knowledge of the twenty-five principles does not occur due to dullness or because the intellect has been impaired by false treatises, that ignorance is "the excessively loud" (*atāratāra*). Furthermore, for someone who, though overwhelmed by internal suffering, feels no agitation regarding *saṃsāra* and thus lacks the desire to know, there is no knowledge; that is "negligence" (*pramāda*).
In this same way, the other two [defilements], "non-rejoicing" (*apramudita*) and "not rejoicing" (*apramodamāna*), are to be understood as applying to the other two [cases] respectively.
Even when instructed by a friend, the lack of certainty regarding the intellect is ignorance; mutual non-attainment is [also] ignorance.

Alternatively, due to the failure to attain [the instruction], or when the guru turns his face away, the failure to achieve knowledge for one of ill fortune is ignorance—that is, ignorance characterized by false joy.
Thus, these eight failures of attainment (asiddhi), which are the opposites of attainment (siddhi), have been explained.
Thus, this twenty-eightfold incapacity has been explained. Here it is asked: what is the ninefold contentment? It is said in response:
having conceptualized *prakṛti* as the ultimate reality, one who becomes completely satisfied attains equanimity; through that contentment, its technical designation in the Tantra is "Ambhas."
Another, having attained contentment by regarding the intellect (*buddhi*) as the ultimate reality, has for that contentment the designation "water" (*śalila*).
Another, having accepted the ego-sense (*ahaṃkāra*) as the ultimate reality and being satisfied with that, has for that contentment the designation "obstruction" (*rodha*).

Yet another, having determined that the subtle elements (*tanmātra*), which are objects of enjoyment, constitute the ultimate reality and being satisfied with that, has for that contentment the designation "rain" (*vṛṣṭi*).
Thus, there are four internal contentments (*tuṣṭi*). In all four of these contentments, however, there is no liberation because the knowledge of reality (*tattvajñāna*) is impossible [to attain].
Upon the cessation of sense objects, five contentments arise through the perception of defects such as the acquisition, preservation, loss, attachment, and injury associated with external objects.

Because one perceives faults in the acquisition of wealth, contentment arises; yet even for such a renunciant, there is no liberation due to the absence of knowledge of reality. This is the fifth contentment, called *sutārā*. Furthermore, because one perceives faults in the preservation of wealth, contentment arises; yet even for such a renunciant, there is no liberation due to the absence of knowledge of reality. This is the sixth contentment, designated as *supārā*.

Another person, being satisfied by seeing the fault of decay in objects, [thinks] that even for one who has renounced there is no liberation due to the absence of knowledge of reality; this is the seventh satisfaction (*tuṣṭi*), called *sunetrā*. Another person, being satisfied by seeing the fault of attachment in objects, [thinks] that even for one who has renounced there is no liberation due to the absence of knowledge of reality; this is the eighth satisfaction, called *sumarīcikā*. Another person, being satisfied by desisting from injury and other faults for the sake of living beings, [thinks] that even for one who has renounced there is no liberation due to the absence of knowledge of reality; this is the ninth satisfaction, called *uttamāmbhasikā*.
Thus, these nine contentments have been explained. Here it is asked: "What are the eight accomplishments?
To this it is said: that knowledge which arises regarding the reality of the elements of existence is the first accomplishment; it is called *tāreya*.
That knowledge which arises through the mere sound of the word regarding the reality of the state of being is called the accomplishment named *sutārā*.
That knowledge which arises through study regarding the reality of the state of being is the third accomplishment, called *tārayantī*.
That knowledge which arises after having dispelled internal suffering regarding the reality of the state of being is the fourth accomplishment, called *pramuditā*.
When knowledge arises regarding the true nature of beings after having dispelled suffering caused by other living beings (*ādhibhautika*), that is the fifth attainment (*siddhi*), called *pramuditā*.

When knowledge arises regarding the true nature of beings after having dispelled suffering caused by divine or supernatural factors (*ādhidaivika*), that is the sixth attainment, called *pramodamānā*. However, when knowledge arises regarding the true nature of beings due to the non-separation from association with the affectionate (*snigdha-saṃsarga*), that is the seventh attainment, called *ramyakā*.
The knowledge that arises through service and giving, when the Guru—who has become one with the reality of the nature of things—is fully satisfied, is called the accomplishment known as "True Joy.
Thus, these eight accomplishments have been explained. [These are the ten root meanings. (Tattvasaṃgraha 16)
Here it is asked: what are the ten topics based on the *Daśamūlika*? To this it is replied:
existence, unity, purposefulness, being for the sake of another, distinctness, lack of agency, conjunction, disjunction, the plurality of spirits, and the continued existence of the body.
These are the ten points concerning the *Daśamūlika*.
By the statement "because the aggregate exists for the sake of another," the existence of the *puruṣa* (spirit) is established.
By the two synonymous arguments—"because there is a finite measure of distinct entities" and "therefore there is an unmanifest cause"—the existence of *pradhāna* (primordial matter) is established.
By the phrase "having a cause and being impermanent," its singularity is established.
By the phrase "consisting of pleasure, pain, and dejection," its purposefulness is established.
By the phrase "by means of various methods," its being for the sake of another is established.
The distinction [between the two] is established by the fact that [Prakṛti] consists of the three guṇas, is non-discriminative, and is an object;
from that very opposite [nature], the non-agency of the Puruṣa is established.
The accomplishment of Yoga is for the sake of the Puruṣa’s perception and likewise for the sake of the isolation (kaivalya) of the Pradhāna.

When the dissolution of the body has occurred, because its purpose has been fulfilled, the accomplishment of separation [from the body] is established. By the phrase "of births, deaths, and instruments," the plurality of Puruṣas is established.
By the phrase "like the whirling of a potter's wheel," the continued existence of the residual impressions is established.
These meanings of the ten roots have been explained.
There are fifty conditions for these ten [roots] and those previously taught.
These sixty categories are called the *Ṣaṣṭitantra*.
[The Emanation of Grace // Tats_17 //] Here it is asked: what is the emanation of grace? To this it is replied:

Having seen that sons produced from the external five subtle elements (*tanmātra*) were devoid of a support, Brahmā, through meditation, created the emanation of grace from those very subtle elements.
[The fourteen-fold creation of beings // Tattvasaṃgraha 18 //] Here someone asks: "What is this fourteen-fold creation of beings? To this it is said:
The divine [creation] is of eight varieties—the Piśāca, Rākṣasa, Yakṣa, Gandharva, Aindra, Prājāpatya, and Brāhma—these being the eight classes of divine beings.
The animal realm is fivefold: domestic animals, birds, wild beasts, reptiles, and plants. Those beginning with cattle and ending with mice are domestic animals (*paśu*).
Those beginning with Garuḍas and ending with mosquitoes are birds (*pakṣin*).
Animals range from lions down to jackals;
reptiles range from snakes down to insects;
and immobile beings range from mountains down to grass.
The human realm consists of a single type, ranging from the Brāhmaṇas down to the Cāṇḍālas;
the divine realm has eight divisions, and the animal kingdom is fivefold;
and the human realm is one—thus, in brief, is the elemental creation.
[The creation of the elements is threefold.

(Tattvasaṃgraha 19)] In brief, regarding those creations which are of three kinds, it is asked: what is the threefold creation of the elements? To this it is replied: "the subtle, those born of mother and father, and the gross.
The group consisting of the five organs of cognition, the vital breaths, the intellect, and the mind is the subtle.
The meaning is "subtle bodies" (*liṅgaśarīra*).

Those born of mother and father consist of six sheaths (*ṣāṭkauśika*); therein, from the mother come hair, blood, and flesh, and from the father come sinews, bones, and marrow—this is the group of six.

The "abundant" refers to the five great elements (*pañcamahābhūta*), wherein jars and other objects are contained within the great elements. Thus, the threefold creation of the constituents (*dhātu*) has been explained.
This is called the mandala of saṃsāra.
[There are three kinds of bondage. (Tattvasaṃgraha 20)] Regarding this, it is asked: "What are the three kinds of bondage? To this it is replied:
they are the bondage of primordial nature (*prakṛti-bandha*), the transformative bondage (*vaikārika-bandha*), and the bondage of sacrificial fees (*dakṣiṇā-bandha*).

Among these, that which is called *prakṛti-bandha* (the bond of primordial nature) refers to the dissolution into nature (*prakṛtilaya*) for one who identifies with the eight constituent principles (*prakṛtis*); this is termed *prakṛti-bandha*.

Therein, that which is called *vaikārika-bandha* (the bond of the modified) refers to the state of those among worldly renunciants who are overcome by the modified senses (*vaikārikendriyas*), who are intensely attached to objects such as sound, whose senses are unsubdued, who are ignorant, and who are deluded by desire;
this is termed *vaikārika-bandha*.

The "bond of sacrificial fees" (*dakṣiṇābandha*) refers to those among students, householders, mendicants, and forest-dwellers whose minds are afflicted by desire and delusion; when they bestow a sacrificial fee preceded by pride, it is called the bond of sacrificial fees.
Thus, the threefold bondage has been explained. And it is said:
Bondage is declared to be threefold: by means of the *prākṛta* (natural) bond, as well as the *vaikārika* (modified) bond, and thirdly, by means of sacrificial fees (*dakṣiṇā*).
[There are three kinds of liberation.
(Tattvasaṃgraha 21)] Regarding this, it is asked: what are the three kinds of liberation?
To this it is replied: through the abundance of knowledge, through the subsiding of passion for the sense-faculties, and through total destruction.

Through the intensification of knowledge and the subsiding of passion for the senses, the destruction of one's own merit and demerit occurs; and from the destruction of merit and demerit, absolute liberation (*kaivalya*) follows.
And it has been said:
"The first liberation is through knowledge, and the second is from the complete exhaustion of passion."
But the third [liberation] results from total destruction; thus has the definition of liberation been explained.
[The means of valid cognition are threefold. (Tattvasaṃgraha 22)] What are these three kinds of means of valid cognition? To this it is said:
perception, inference, and authoritative testimony—these are the three kinds of means of valid cognition.
First, "the seen" (dṛṣṭa) is explained: that which consists of the five objects of the senses is indeed "the seen.
Inference (anumāna) is the means of valid cognition consisting of knowledge arising from the observation of a mark (liṅga);
for example, rain is established by the rising of clouds, water by rows of cranes, and fire by smoke—that is inference.
An object that cannot be established by means of perception or inference is established through the word of a reliable authority (*āptavacana*).
For example: "Indra is the king of the gods; the Northern Kurus exist; Mount Meru is golden; and there are celestial nymphs (*apsaras*) in heaven.

These beings such as Indra, which cannot be established by perception or inference, are spoken of by sages such as Vasiṣṭha and others, saying, "Indra and the rest do exist," and thus scripture (*āgama*) also exists.
One who is devoted to his own duty, free from attachment and aversion,
possessed of knowledge, perfected in ethical conduct— such a person should be known as a trustworthy authority.
Thus, these three kinds of valid cognition have been explained.

Here it is asked: what is established by those three kinds of valid cognition? To this it is replied: just as in the world grains are measured by means of measures such as the *prastha* and so forth; [so too is the object of knowledge established by the three types of valid cognition].
Just as substances such as sandalwood are weighed by a scale, so too are the things that constitute reality measured by this [means].
Overwhelmed by the three kinds of suffering, the Brahmin sought refuge with the great seer Kapila; regarding this, it is said:
[The threefold suffering. (Tattvasaṃgraha 23)] What are the three kinds of suffering? To this it is replied:
internal, external, and celestial.
In that regard, internal [suffering] is of two kinds: physical and mental.
That which occurs in the body is physical; that which occurs in the mind is mental.
Among these, what is called physical refers to the suffering that arises from the imbalance of wind, bile, and phlegm—such as fever, diarrhea, cholera, and fainting—and this is termed physical.
Desire, anger, greed, delusion, intoxication, envy, and so forth, as well as separation from the beloved and the like, are called mental (*mānasa*).
That which arises from other beings is "pertaining to beings" (*ādhibhautika*);
the suffering that arises from humans, domestic animals, wild beasts, reptiles, and stationary plants is *ādhibhautika*.
That which arises from the divine powers is *ādhidaivika*.
Whatever suffering arises caused by cold, heat, wind, rain, the combination of these elements, and so forth, that is *ādhidaivika*.
In a Brahmin overwhelmed by these three kinds of suffering, the desire to know (*jijñāsā*) has arisen.
The desire to know is *jijñāsā*.
Just as thirst is the desire of one who is thirsty to drink water, so too,
in brief, is the knowledge of the supreme good (*niḥśreyasa*).
"Knowing which, there shall be no further birth."
This is the knowledge of the great seer Kapila, the high-souled one;
having heard which, the brahmin then attained the highest good and felt his purpose fulfilled.
This *Kramadīpikā* has been explained according to the sequence of the *Sāṃkhyasūtras*;
it should be known that here there are three hundred verses in the *anuṣṭubh* meter.
Thus ends the commentary on the aphorisms known as the *Śrītattvasamāsa*.
